summary: Defines Link Quality Monitoring for PPP, a way for each end of a PPP link to learn how well the link is carrying data. It was replaced by RFC 1989.

eli5.summary: Imagine two people on a walkie-talkie checking how many words got through. PPP link quality monitoring does that to see if a line is good or noisy.

questions: how to measure ppp link quality
how to detect data loss on ppp links
subtitle: Protocol for measuring data loss and link quality on point-to-point connections.

tldr.problem: Network operators needed a way to continuously measure the quality of point-to-point links and detect data loss without losing the ability to implement different recovery policies at each end.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1333 defines the Link-Quality-Report (LQR) packet, a mechanism for each end of a PPP link to periodically exchange counters of packets and octets sent, received, and discarded, enabling each end to compute packet loss rates.
tldr.outcome: LQM became a standard way for PPP implementations to monitor link quality but was superseded by RFC 1989 with improvements and clarifications.

today: RFC 1333 is obsoleted by RFC 1989, which provides clarifications and improvements to PPP link quality monitoring. PPP itself remains widely used, especially for broadband access, though modern monitoring techniques have supplemented or replaced LQM in some contexts.

sections.title: The Problem and the Approach
sections.content:
Data communication links are never perfect. Noise, equipment failures, buffer overruns, and congestion can cause packets to be dropped or corrupted. Network equipment sometimes needs to know when a link is degrading so it can take action—perhaps by routing traffic through an alternate path or temporarily disconnecting until quality improves.

RFC 1333 separates the Link Quality Monitoring problem into two parts: a mechanism (how to measure link quality) and a policy (how to react to bad quality). The RFC fully specifies the mechanism—the Link-Quality-Report packet and the procedure for sending it—but deliberately does not mandate a policy. Different implementations can measure the same link quality data but react differently, allowing flexibility and experimentation.
sections.eli5: The RFC specifies a measurement tool (the LQR packet) but lets each router decide what counts as 'too bad' and what to do about it. This keeps the protocol simple and vendors free to innovate.

sections.title: Counters and Measurements
sections.content:
Link Quality Monitoring relies on counters that track the amount of data passing over the link. Each end maintains counters for packets and octets transmitted and successfully received. The RFC defines three internal counters in addition to those from MIB-II (the SNMP system counters). OutLQRs counts transmitted Link-Quality-Report packets. InLQRs counts received LQR packets. InGoodOctets counts octets in successfully received frames (excluding frames that were discarded or had errors).

These counters are relative, not absolute: they increase monotonically but are not synchronized across the link. By comparing the values in successive LQR packets, each end can compute the change (or 'delta') in packets and octets over a measurement interval. Comparing these deltas lets each end calculate the loss rate on each direction of the link independently.
sections.eli5: Each end keeps a running tally: how many packets I sent, how many I got back. When they swap tallies, they can compute: 'I sent 100 packets but you only got 95. That's a 5 percent loss.'

sections.title: Packet Format and Transmission
sections.content:
The Link-Quality-Report packet is encapsulated in PPP frames with protocol number 0xc025 (hex). Each LQR contains twelve 32-bit fields. The first group (LastOutLQRs, LastOutPackets, LastOutOctets) echoes back the peer's output counters from the previous LQR, allowing the peer to see what we received. The second group (PeerIn*) reports what we received from the peer, and the third group (PeerOut*) reports our own transmission counts. A fourth group (SaveIn*) is logically appended by the receiver to record its own receive counters at the time of reception.

LQRs are typically sent at a negotiated interval (the default is every 5 to 30 seconds). If the link is good, LQRs can be sent less frequently to minimize overhead. If loss is detected, implementations may increase the frequency of LQRs to get finer-grained measurements. If a duplicate LQR is received (same PeerInLQRs value), an LQR is generated immediately, signaling that something is out of sync.
sections.eli5: An LQR packet says: 'I sent these many packets, received these many from you, and your last message said you received this many from me.' The receiver stamps the arrival time and echoes it back in the next LQR.

sections.title: Negotiation and Configuration
sections.content:
Link Quality Monitoring is negotiated during the PPP Link Control Protocol (LCP) Establishment phase. The Quality-Protocol Configuration Option specifies which quality monitoring protocol to use (only Link-Quality-Report is defined here) and the Reporting-Period: the maximum time (in hundredths of seconds) between LQR transmissions. A value of zero indicates that the peer should respond immediately to each LQR rather than maintain a timer, placing the burden of driving the exchange on the other end.

The negotiation is directional: one end may request LQRs from the peer while the other does not. The peer is obligated to send LQRs if asked, even if it does not request them in return. This asymmetry simplifies implementations that need monitoring on one direction but can afford to not send measurements themselves.
sections.eli5: During setup, the two ends negotiate: 'Please send me a status report every 10 seconds.' The other end may or may not ask for reports back. Once negotiated, the process runs automatically.

sections.title: Computing Link Quality and Failure Detection
sections.content:
Upon receiving an LQR, the Link-Manager can compute the delta between the current and previous report. If the current PeerInLQRs field is zero, the peer has not yet received any LQRs from us; the measurement cannot proceed until synchronization occurs. The LastOutLQRs field can be directly compared with PeerInLQRs to count lost LQRs. The change in PeerInPackets can be compared with the change in LastOutPackets to determine packet loss on the outbound link, and similarly for incoming loss using SaveInPackets versus PeerOutPackets.

The RFC provides policy suggestions but does not mandate them. When loss is detected, it is recommended to avoid bouncing the link up and down by using hysteresis: require K successes out of N measurement intervals before declaring the link good. Upon detecting consistently poor quality, implementations may close Network Layer protocols (causing IP to disconnect) while continuing to send LQRs, allowing recovery once the link improves.
sections.eli5: The math is simple: compare what I said I sent with what you say you received. The difference is loss. If loss persists, consider another route. If it recovers, reconnect.
